label: Polyhedral Complexes of Bounded Curvature
notes: This chapter glues finitely many shapes from the model space M_k along isometric faces and asks when the result has curvature at most k. The whole story compresses into one local-to-global slogan: control the geometry around each vertex, then let Cartan-Hadamard upgrade local curvature to global CAT(k).

label: M_k-Polyhedral Complexes
notes: A polyhedral complex is built from convex cells in the model space of constant curvature k, glued along isometric faces with finitely many isometry types of cell. Bridson shows the gluing carries an honest length metric, so geodesics and angles between adjacent cells are well defined.

label: The Link of a Vertex
notes: The link records all directions emanating from a vertex. Each cell containing the vertex contributes a spherical simplex whose side lengths are the angles between faces, and these glue into a metric simplicial complex. The link is the infinitesimal sphere encoding how cells fan out around the point.

label: Curvature is Local
notes: Curvature bounded above is intrinsically a local statement, so for a complex it is decided cell by cell, and the only places where trouble can hide are the vertices. Away from a vertex every point already sits inside a CAT(k) neighbourhood inherited from the model cells.

label: Gromov's Link Condition
notes: This is the central theorem of the chapter. An M_k-complex with the finiteness hypothesis is locally CAT(k) exactly when every vertex link is a CAT(1) space. The angular geometry of directions controls metric curvature, converting an analytic bound into a single condition on each link.

label: Large Links and 2 pi
notes: For a CAT(1) space the operative obstruction is short closed geodesics. The link of every vertex must contain no closed geodesic of length strictly less than two pi. We say the links are large; a loop shorter than two pi is exactly a missing turning corner that would let geodesics branch.

label: Why 2 pi
notes: A closed geodesic of length below two pi in the link reflects a direction pair joined by two short angular routes, which unfolds into a digon and ruins comparison-triangle convexity. The two pi threshold is the spherical signature of CAT(1), so it is the precise frontier where the curvature bound can break.

label: Cube Complexes
notes: In the cubical case the model cells are Euclidean unit cubes with k equal to zero, and every angle between faces is a right angle. The link of a vertex is then an all-right-angled spherical complex, which is the same data as an abstract simplicial complex. The geometry becomes combinatorics.

label: Flag Links
notes: Gromov's combinatorial criterion: a cube complex is locally CAT(0) precisely when every vertex link is a flag simplicial complex. Flag means every set of pairwise adjacent vertices already spans a simplex, so there are no empty triangles. This is a purely finite check on the link graph.

label: No Empty Squares
notes: An empty square is three cubes around an edge with the fourth missing, producing a length three loop in the link, well under two pi. Filling it is exactly the flag condition. The cartoon to keep: an empty square is forbidden, while the filled corner cube certifies non-positive curvature.

label: Cartan-Hadamard and Examples
notes: Combining the local link condition with Cartan-Hadamard, a complete, simply connected, locally CAT(0) complex is globally CAT(0). For finite complexes this means checking flagness of finitely many links produces genuine CAT(0) cube complexes, a rich and computable source of non-positively curved spaces and groups.

label: Recap and the Workflow
notes: The workflow is a ladder: model cells fix local geometry, links translate curvature into angular data, the link condition becomes flagness in the cubical case, and Cartan-Hadamard globalises. Checking one finite combinatorial property at each vertex now certifies that an entire group acts on a CAT(0) space.
